Firefighers and emergency services close to Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Wainwright, Alberta, Canada [Megan Albu/AFP]By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and ReutersPublished On 23 Oct 202623 Oct 2026
A fire that killed four soldiers at a western Canadian military base was sparked by an exercise using live grenades, a military official said.
The deadly fire broke out on a grenade launcher range during military exercises on Saturday, with high winds propelling it across the base, Brigadier-General Vanessa Hanrahan, commander of the Canadian Forces Military Police Group, told reporters on Thursday.
“A subsequent change in wind direction and velocity significantly increased the fire’s intensity,” she added, with the flames spreading to a training area at the Wainwright military base in Alberta.
Due to the blaze being in the “permanent danger area” of the range, firefighters were unable to directly combat it, Hanrahan added.
The fire spread on Saturday afternoon during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
The military base lies in the prairies, a landscape of wide, open grasslands, rolling plains and scattered groves of trees.
About 84 soldiers were split between a grenade range and an area where they practised attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second training area.
Four soldiers died and 39 were injured, with 27 requiring hospitalisation. The incident was one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military.
The soldiers and reserve members were participating in exercises ahead of a planned deployment to Latvia, where Canadian forces have their largest international military operation. Advertisement

Welfare check on elephant Madhubala at the new enclosure in Karachi Safari Park, Karachi, Pakistan, October 10, 2026 [Courtesy of Four Paws]By Alia ChughtaiPublished On 23 Oct 202623 Oct 2026
At Karachi Zoo, Jude Allen sang, You Are My Sunshine, to an elephant he could not save.
Noor Jehan, the 17-year-old African elephant, was suffering. Allen recalls massaging her legs, nursing her bedsores and spending her final days beside her.
She died on April 22, 2023, surrounded by a few activists. Allen, 45, had held various corporate jobs while volunteering as an animal caregiver since an early age.
But Noor Jehan changed something in him, he said. “The day this wild African elephant rested her painful forehead on mine, and I hugged her for the first time – it all made sense,” he tells Al Jazeera.
“I quit my job without a plan B.”
Now three years later, Allen has turned the grief of Noor Jehan’s loss into care for one of her sisters, Madhubala, who also faces major health challenges. He is part of a growing campaign of Pakistani and international activists and doctors trying to save Madhubala, a victim, her carers say, not just of medical conditions, but also of a system that is simply unable to give animals in captivity the attention and facilities they need.African elephants Madhubala, left, and Malika roam with a caretaker inside the premises of Safari Park in Karachi on October 9, 2026 [Rizwan Tabassum/AFP]
The elephant sisters
In 2009, four elephant calves captured in Tanzania were brought to Pakistan, allegedly through an animal trader.

US tech stocks have dropped sharply amid market jitters over the sustainability of companies’ enormous capital investments in AI.
The Nasdaq Composite, which is dominated by tech firms linked to the AI boom, fell 2.6 percent on Thursday, its steepest fall since the index tumbled 4.2 percent on June 5.

The broader S&P 500 slid 1.21 percent, the benchmark’s biggest drop since a 1.52 percent decline on July 29.
Apart from Apple, each of the “Magnificent 7”, which make up more than one-third of the overall market, saw substantial losses.
Meta dropped nearly 7 percent after it raised its projected capital spending for this year to $135bn to $145bn in its latest earnings report, even as the Facebook parent company’s net profit fell short of expectations.
Amazon fell 4.6 percent, while Nvidia dropped 4.4 percent.
Tesla and Alphabet both fell 3.1 percent, while Microsoft declined 2.2 percent.
Apple rose 1.2 percent.
The sell-off extended to other major tech players, including Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, both of which fell about 8 percent, and Broadcom, which slid 4.3 percent.
After the losses, the Nasdaq is about 5.8 percent off its all-time high, reached on October 6.

Spearheading that campaign is Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a federal agency housed in the Department of Homeland Security.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Trump administration sues California over noncitizens on voter rollslist 2 of 3Key takeaways from Donald Trump’s controversial speech on election securitylist 3 of 3Homeland Security Secretary Mullin reiterates Trump threats about electionsend of list
Under Trump, the agency has grown substantially, boasting 22,000 officers and agents as of January, a staffing increase of 120 percent.
Thanks to recent spending packages, ICE is also considered the best-funded federal law enforcement agency in the US.
But the agency, founded in 2003, has come under increased scrutiny for its aggressive tactics and expedited hiring techniques.
Immigration agents, under the authority of ICE and other agencies, have been responsible for at least 25 shootings since the start of Trump’s second term, six of which have been fatal. At least 60 people have also died in ICE custody since January 2025.
That track record has made democracy advocates and human rights groups worried about ICE’s activities in the lead-up to the November 3 midterm elections.
Organisations like Human Rights Watch and the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) have voiced concern that the Trump administration could use ICE to intimidate voters.

United States President Donald Trump has said that tech mogul Elon Musk has restored Ukraine’s access to Starlink, a satellite internet service that plays a key role in Kyiv’s war effort and air defences.
On Thursday, Trump declined to discuss a report from The Wall Street Journal that he had called Musk and instructed him to end restrictions on Ukraine’s connection.

The news outlet reported that Starlink services returned to normal following the call.
“I don’t want to comment on it, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn’t make any difference, I guess. The bottom line, he put it back,” Trump told reporters when asked about the report.
On October 13, Ukrainian officials announced that sudden restrictions on Starlink services had left the country’s military scrambling.
Though the system came back online, connectivity has reportedly remained spotty.
Questions have persisted about where the decision to restrict access came from, with Musk and the Trump administration officials trading blame.
Trump has denied ordering restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starlink.
“Well, I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” he said on Friday. “And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”
